description: We're ZenithCode, a small team that likes building things that actually get used. Most of what we make starts with a simple question: what happens to the people who can't count on help arriving quickly? Sometimes that leads to an app, sometimes a website, sometimes a video. We learn a lot along the way, we argue over details, and we keep at it until it works.
summary: Higia is an autonomous health-monitoring system for astronauts living in long-duration habitats on the Moon or Mars. It combines vital signs, symptoms the astronaut reports by voice, on-board tests and mission context, and evaluates them with 38 rules grounded in NASA's Human Research Program, covering its 17 health risks plus venous thromboembolism. Everything critical runs offline on the device; AI only adds capabilities. What sets it apart is how it communicates: it compares each reading with the crew member's personal baseline, tailors the message to who receives it, picks the right channel (shared screen, personal screen or headset, never exposing private data), respects sleep and, if an alert gets no response, notifies crewmates, the onboard doctor, the base or Earth together with the medical history. With up to 22-minute delays to Mars, crews cannot rely on Earth: Higia gives them back the autonomy to assess their health and act in time.
details:
PROJECT DETAILS: HIGIA, an autonomous health-monitoring system for astronauts

What it does and how it works

Higia is a health assistant for crews living in long-duration habitats on the Moon or Mars. It also works on a station, a spacecraft or a rover. It collects health indicators, decides what they mean for this astronaut in this context, explains it in plain language, and acts if nobody responds.

Input. Higia accepts more than 50 types of data in 7 families:
Vital signs, including the six indicators suggested by the challenge: blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep hours and mood.
Symptoms the astronaut reports by voice (“Higia, last night I slept five hours and I feel tired”).
Guided on-board tests: a cognitive assessment, reaction time (PVT), isometric grip strength, the Valsalva maneuver and an orientation check.
Suit sensors, such as helmet impact in g and pre-breathe minutes.
Environment and lab data: radiation dose, cabin oxygen, noise, microbial load and urinary calcium.

Input can come from voice, text, clicks, the camera or the built-in mission simulator.

Detection. 38 rules cover all 17 health risks of NASA’s Human Research Program plus venous thromboembolism, 18 in total. Every rule:
cites its scientific source;
compares readings with the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline;
takes context into account: habitat, EVA or rover; orbit, Moon or Mars; activity, solar storms and time of day.

For example, 125 bpm during exercise is not an alarm. When four or more mild signals appear across three or more body systems, Higia combines them into a warning that advises against an EVA, even if no single signal is serious.

Communication. The same finding is worded differently for each person:
a veteran doctor gets technical figures;
a novice engineer prone to panic gets calm, number-free guidance.

Higia also picks the channel: shared screen, personal screen or suit headset. Private data never goes to a shared screen, and warnings wait until the astronaut wakes up.

Escalation. Every alert asks the astronaut to confirm “I’m OK”. If there is no answer within 30 s (15 s when the condition could incapacitate them), Higia warns by voice first. It then contacts the nearest crewmate, the on-board doctor, the base and Earth, in that order, sending what happened, the astronaut’s location and their medical history. If no one is reachable, it activates a beacon.
Offline first. All critical logic runs on the device with no connection. AI only adds natural conversation, an AI assessment of each finding and camera analysis of hazards. Urgent commands such as “call for help” never wait for the AI or the network.

The interface includes:

a clickable anatomical figure with organ, muscle and bone layers, front and back, colored by status;
a “Why this message?” panel showing the exact data used, the baseline, the NASA risk and the channel chosen;
mini trend charts and a fitness-for-task panel (EVA, piloting, intense exercise);
an editable medical history and HL7 FHIR export for medical systems;
a simulator with 42 mission scenarios and a live matrix showing coverage of all 18 NASA risks.

Benefits

Astronauts: early detection against their own baseline, messages they understand without being alarmed, privacy for mental health, and guaranteed help even when they cannot ask for it.
Flight surgeons: traceable reports with the exact data behind each finding, the medical history attached to every emergency, standard FHIR format, and less noise because Higia only speaks when a risk level changes.
The mission: EVAs and piloting are discouraged before an accident happens, the crew stays autonomous despite 3–22 minute delays to Mars, and the network is never a single point of failure.

Intended impact

We want to show that a health system can be autonomous, explainable and humane at the same time, and that how you communicate a finding matters as much as detecting it. The next steps are:

validate the thresholds with physicians and physiotherapists;
connect real wearables;
add measurement routines and gamification;
test Higia in Earth analogs of isolated missions.

The same features that make Higia useful on Mars (offline, no doctor needed, automatic escalation) also help on Earth: Antarctic bases, remote rural areas, submarines and offshore platforms, and elderly people who live alone.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Language and interface: TypeScript, React 18, our own CSS design system and our own SVG icons.
Build and testing: Vite 5, Node.js, Zod for validation and Vitest (230 automated tests, all passing).
Speech recognition: the Web Speech API, plus Vosk running in WebAssembly with a Spanish model, fully offline.
Voice: Piper neural text-to-speech with ONNX Runtime Web, generated on the device.
Optional AI: the DeepSeek API (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) for conversation, assessments and vision.
Interoperability: HL7 FHIR Observation export.
Browser features: microphone, camera, IndexedDB and a Service Worker so the app can be installed.
Development: Git and GitHub. We used Claude (Anthropic) to assist with code and documentation.
Hardware: a laptop, microphone, speakers and webcam. Sensors are simulated with realistic ranges and units so they can be replaced by real devices.

How it is creative

Higia changes the question from “what do the numbers say?” to “who needs to know, how and where?”
It speaks each crew member’s language, so the same fact produces four different messages.
It does not stay silent: an unanswered alert turns into automatic outreach to the crew, the base or Earth.
It sees what no single signal shows by combining mild signals across body systems.
It has a visible presence: the screen edge glows when it hears “Higia”, and it asks questions on its own, such as a quick cognitive check or how the astronaut slept.
Nothing is a black box: every message shows its data, its thresholds and its NASA source.
The simulator turns the whole mission into a testbed, and each of its 42 scenarios is also an automated test.

Factors we considered

Communication delay and no doctor on board. Higia does not assume real-time help from Earth. This follows NASA’s risk of inadequate systems-operations support (§7.2.4).
Astronauts are not doctors. It gives plain explanations, step-by-step guides and no jargon.
Alarm fatigue. It only speaks when a level changes, sends reminders based on experience and respects sleep.
Privacy. Mental health and team-cohesion data are sensitive; reports use an ID instead of a name; the AI never receives the astronaut’s name; the offline voice engine keeps audio on the device.
Safety. Urgent actions run locally first, the AI can only request actions from a closed list that the app validates, and every alert includes steps (the tests check this).
Differences between people. Every comparison uses a personal baseline.
Different environments. Habitat, EVA and rover, in orbit, on the Moon or on Mars, each with its own delays and thresholds.
Accessibility. Color is always paired with text, there is full keyboard and screen-reader support, and the app respects reduced-motion settings.
Scientific grounding and honesty. Every rule cites the HRP, all thresholds are marked provisional until clinically validated, and Higia is a prototype, not a medical device.
